title: LSAR: Sparse Lexical Representation Learning for Efficient and Interpretable Audio Retrieval

problem.claim: Audio retrieval must reconcile lexical precision, non-verbal acoustic evidence, and efficient, transparent retrieval.

gap.claim: Existing cascaded ASR pipelines discard non-verbal cues and amplify recognition errors, while dense retrievers reduce inspectability and incur indexing and query-time overhead.

contributions.claim: LSAR maps audio directly into a sparse lexical space compatible with inverted-index search.
LSAR uses cross-modal sparse alignment and complementary branches to model spoken content, acoustic context, and logic associations with explicit term activations.
LSAR supports direct audio retrieval without an ASR transcription stage and is intended as an index-friendly first-stage retriever for multimodal retrieval.

author_reported_evidence.claim: Experiments on diverse benchmarks covering speech, captioning, and audio question answering show that LSAR maps continuous audio representations into a sparse lexical space.
The authors report that LSAR enables high-recall candidate retrieval with low latency and significantly narrows the search space.
The authors report keyword-level interpretability for the resulting retrieval representation.

narrative_sequence.summary: Audio retrieval is positioned as a needed component of retrieval-augmented generation, recommendation, and multimedia search.
Existing systems struggle to combine lexical precision, non-verbal acoustic evidence, efficiency, and transparency.
ASR-based cascaded pipelines retrieve over text but amplify recognition errors and lose non-verbal cues; dense retrievers avoid transcription but reduce inspectability and add computational overhead.
LSAR directly maps audio into a sparse lexical space using cross-modal alignment and multiple branches, enabling inverted-index retrieval without ASR.
Benchmark experiments report sparse lexical mapping, high-recall low-latency first-stage retrieval, reduced search space, and keyword-level interpretability.

source_observation.claim: The proposed representation combines explicit sparse term activations with direct audio input.

interpretation.claim: A shared sparse lexical interface can connect non-text inputs to mature inverted-index retrieval infrastructure while retaining inspectable activations.

application.claim: Multimodal retrieval systems could use sparse lexical representations as an efficient and interpretable first-stage candidate-generation layer.

exception.claim: The abstract does not establish whether this approach outperforms all dense or ASR-based alternatives across deployment settings.

unknowns: No quantitative benchmark results, metrics, or baseline comparisons are provided.
The abstract does not specify the training data, model architecture details, indexing configuration, or latency measurements.
The abstract does not establish independent verification of the reported findings.
